new.title: A Study of the 30 May 2026 Meteor Event Employing Data from Raspberry Boom Infrasound Sensors in the Boston Area
new.summary: Infrasound signals of one and a half cycles of a 0.4 Hz pressure pulse were detected from the 30 May 2026 meteor over Cape Cod Bay at several university and private Raspberry Boom sensors in the Greater Boston area. Our analyses of these signals demonstrate the ability to define directivity to the source of the event based on differences in the timing of the signals, to determine its identity and location by analysis of the relationship between event distance and sensor event timing, and event acoustical power by the infrasonic pressures measured at the sensor sites. The infrasound event is determined to be the atmospheric fireball blast at between 40 and 50 km in altitude with acoustic energy on the order of 5% to 14% of the total fireball energy.

new.title: The Impact of Orbital Data Centers on the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory
new.summary: As the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory begins its Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), satellite operators are racing to launch Orbital Data Center (ODC) satellites into low-Earth orbit. We present an impact assessment of a simulated $\sim$1 million ODC satellite constellation, arranged per recent filings across two low-Earth and two Sun-synchronous orbit regimes, on one year of Rubin Observatory LSST observations. Our six-stage sequential pipeline combines orbit propagation, field-of-view matching, observer-frame geometry, brightness modeling, surface-brightness calculations, and pixel-loss estimates. We find that on a given night, up to 80% of LSST pointings would contain at least one illuminated ODC satellite streak, depending on the time of year. The yearly average of contaminated exposures is closer to 20%, due to seasonal visibility variations and bright satellite streaks being most prominent near twilight. Sun-synchronous ODCs disproportionately contaminate due to preferential illumination geometry. The ODC satellite brightness distribution is multi-modal, where solar panel specular reflection can appear as bright as 2-4 AB mag ($\mu_g \approx 9-11$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$), while diffuse reflections more typically reach 6 AB mag ($\mu_g \approx 13-14$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$). Even at 10% deployment, the constellation would still produce widespread visible streak contamination throughout the year. ODC satellites would also drastically increase sky brightness -- by more than 1000% near twilight with no Moon. Launching and operating ODC satellites at this scale would significantly harm LSST science, including typical 5-10% nightly mean pixel losses near twilight, even if multiple mitigation strategies are implemented.

new.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks vs U-Net: Application to thermal dust emission recovery in the microwave
new.summary: Galactic thermal dust emission is the dominant foreground contaminant of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) at frequencies above 100 GHz, and its accurate separation is essential for current and future CMB experiments. Deep learning methods, in particular convolutional architectures such as the U-Net, have demonstrated strong performance for CMB component separation, but typically operate as purely data-driven models with no explicit enforcement of the physical laws governing the emission they reconstruct. In this work, we present a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) that embeds the Modified Black Body (MBB) spectral model as a hard, differentiable architectural constraint, and we compare it against a standard U-Net baseline trained under an identical pipeline. Both architectures are trained on realistic simulated Planck HFI patches at four frequencies (143, 217, 353 and 545 GHz) and evaluated on a shared validation set as well as on three independent Galactic dust realizations from the PySM phenomenological dust models named D4, D7 and D10. We find that both networks achieve comparable reconstruction quality across all evaluated datasets, with a Structural Similarity Index Measure consistently above 0.96 and a fitted angular power-spectrum spectral index that agrees with the input to within 1% in every region. Embedding the physical constraint in the PINN does not measurably degrade reconstruction accuracy relative to the unconstrained U-Net, while additionally guaranteeing that every predicted output corresponds to a thermodynamically admissible physical configuration. These results establish the physics-informed formulation as a viable methodological alternative for dust component separation, providing physical interpretability without a trade-off in reconstruction fidelity.

new.title: Listening to the Standard Candles: A Survey-Scale Search for Phase-Coded Beacons in Cepheids, RR~Lyrae and $β$~Cephei Stars
new.summary: Learned et al. (2008) proposed that a civilization could use Cepheids and RR Lyrae stars, the most closely watched clocks in astronomy, as beacons, firing pulsations early with a particle beam to write a message into the timing residuals. The one search to date examined a single Kepler star. We describe Star SETI, an automated pipeline that selects Cepheids, RR Lyrae and $\beta$ Cephei stars from Gaia DR3, measures per-cycle (TESS, Kepler) or block-averaged (ASAS-SN, ZTF) observed-minus-computed timing residuals, tests them for non-white structure, decodes them as a bit stream under the cumulative (``staircase'') modulation of a one-sided trigger, and matches the words to catalogs of recognizable sequences. A resonant antineutrino beam grazing the base of the driving zone needs hundreds to tens of thousands of times less power than a central beam, and driving an RR Lyrae star takes most of its light. Injections into real light curves show that only RR Lyrae stars are detectable near the amplitude that Learned et al. proposed, with half of the codes recovered at 0.2--0.4 per cent of a period per bit in TESS; the ground-based surveys detect only codes held for tens of cycles per bit and decode none. We time 97,725 light curves of 77,596 stars and vet 38,230 timing anomalies; 6823 have timing structure that the vetting cannot attribute to a known cause, all but eight of them on block-averaged timing to which only part of the vetting applies. The highest-ranked are non-radial modes in first-overtone RR Lyrae stars, Blazhko modulation and mode beating in $\beta$ Cephei stars, and no decoded word survives a false-discovery correction. We find no beacon. That bounds only beacons: a perfectly compressed message is indistinguishable from noise, so a civilization communicating efficiently rather than advertising could leave residuals that pass all of our tests, in stars that we cannot single out.

new.title: The SDSS-V Local Volume Mapper (LVM): Technical Overview
new.summary: The Sloan Digital Sky Survey V (SDSS-V) Local Volume Mapper (LVM) is an ultra-wide integral field spectroscopic survey of the Milky Way, the Magellanic Clouds, and a sample of galaxies in the local volume. The LVM spatially resolved spectroscopy covers the bulk of the optical range (3600-9800 A) at medium spectral-resolution (R = 2200-5500), and maps the disks of these galaxies at high physical spatial resolution (< 1 pc in the MW and ~10 pc in the Magellanic Clouds). Observations are carried out with the LVM Instrument (LVM-I), a custom-built robotic telescope, instrument, and facility located at Las Campanas Observatory (LCO) in Chile. In this article we present a technical overview of the LVM project. We describe the hardware, the survey observing strategy, and the details of how science and calibration observations are carried out. We provide a high-level overview of the survey data flow, including the reduction and calibration of the LVM spectra, and the production of the main data products that are released by the project. We also present an assessment of the LVM data quality and instrumental stability based on science observations. The main goal of this article is to serve as a primer for LVM users, providing the technical information required for the adequate analysis, modeling, and interpretation of the LVM data.

new.title: FacilityAudit-Agent: Beyond Mention-as-Usage for Fine-Grained Facility Contribution Attribution in Astrophysics Publications
new.summary: Observatory bibliographies increasingly need to determine not only whether a facility is named in a paper, but how its data support the scientific argument. We frame this need as semantic contribution attribution on a six-level scale (L0-L5), from non-use and mention-only cases to auxiliary, major, and exclusive data support. We present FacilityAudit-Agent, a framework that builds a page-bounded outline of each PDF, enriches sections with roles and facility mentions, and uses a tool-calling large language model (LLM) to fetch text on demand. Evidence from the sections is combined through an explicit decision tree and a coverage-calibrated confidence score, with uncertain cases routed to human review. The framework supports both single-facility and inventory audits and transfers to new facilities without retraining. On a test set of 39,358 human-annotated paper-facility pairs, FacilityAudit-Agent achieves 89.1% accuracy and 79.8% macro-F1 in single_audit mode, outperforming the other three baselines by 5.8, 8.3, and 12.1 accuracy points, respectively, with the clearest gains at L2 and L5. In inventory_audit mode, it also leads in facility listing and in level assignment among listed pairs. Ablations show multi-hop reading and tree indexing matter most for L3-L5. FacilityAudit-Agent has been deployed at the National Astronomical Data Center, where it is responsible for processing publications related to LAMOST, FAST, and EP.

new.title: The MIRI/MRS Library. III. Detector-based optimal spectral extraction and high-contrast imaging applications
new.summary: (Abridged) JWST has now been operational for five years, and the associated data reduction pipelines have reached maturity. For MIRI/MRS, one can generally get a good-quality spectrum by simply running the standard pipeline, especially for unresolved sources. However, users are starting to look deeper into the data, trying to detect the smallest features in the faintest objects, and find close companions. Following the corrections derived in Papers I and II in this series, we now introduce a novel way to extract MIRI/MRS spectra: from the detectors directly. Currently the most common way to analyse data from integral field spectrometers is to reconstruct a spectral cube from the detector images. Theoretically, detector-extracted spectra could reach higher S/N, and better handle bad pixels. We generate stable and well-sampled PSF models using the sub-pixel scan of calibration star 10 Lac observed in PID 3779. These PSFs were used in a detector-based optimal extraction algorithm building on past approaches, where the contributions per pixel were weighted by their noise properties and contribution to the total illumination. The PSF models were used to subtract the PSF of a bright central source from the detector, both by direct subtraction, and a PCA approach. We find that our optimal setup allows us to get a $>$1.5 times higher S/N compared to the standard pipeline cube extraction. However, we approximately matched more involved cube processing. We were able to subtract the PSF to sub-percent levels, allowing us to extract spectra from faint companions. The novel approach greatly improves on the current standard pipeline reduction. We have not yet reached the fundamental noise limits. There are clear points of improvement that can be addressed using additional data. We demonstrate that detector-based processing of MIRI/MRS data has great potential.

new.title: Systematic Slopes in NIRSpec BOTS Observations
new.summary: We investigate empirical white light and spectroscopic trends in the temporal systematic slopes seen in NIRSpec Bright Object Time Series (BOTS) observations. Using a sample of 14 high-resolution G395H (dispersed across both the NRS1 and NRS2 detectors) and 10 low-resolution Prism (dispersed across NRS1 only) transit light curves, we measured the visit-long, pre-transit, and post-transit slopes. For the G395H white light curves, we find a correlation between the G395H NRS1 systematic slope and the host star magnitude, as well as the number of groups per integration. We also note that the systematic slopes vary with time over the course of a given time-series, with steeper pre-transit slopes compared to post-transit. These trends in the white light slopes are not apparent for G395H NRS2 or Prism. At the spectroscopic light curve level, the NRS1 and Prism slopes show a distinct wavelength-dependent signature across the full sample with the largest slopes between ~3-3.4 microns. At these wavelengths, the brightest targets display the strongest chromatic slope signatures. The NRS2 slopes show no apparent chromaticity across the full sample.

cross.title: FastSpec: Fast and versatile stellar spectrum synthesis code
cross.summary: Modelling data from modern spectroscopic surveys and time-resolved spectropolarimetric observations requires stellar synthetic spectra to be computed rapidly over wide wavelength ranges from line lists that increasingly reach hundreds of millions of transitions. Spectropolarimetric analyses of magnetically active stars additionally demand a solution of the polarised radiative transfer problem. We present FastSpec, a new LTE spectrum synthesis code designed around two goals: increased raw computational speed and broad astrophysical applicability, including the calculation of the full Stokes vector in the presence of a magnetic field. FastSpec computes emergent intensity and flux spectra from plane-parallel and spherical model atmospheres. Chemical and ionisation equilibrium is obtained from the updated SME equation-of-state package, continuum opacities follow the ATLAS family of routines, hydrogen bound-bound and bound-free absorption uses the occupation-probability formalism, and line absorption is evaluated with fast table-based Voigt and Faraday-Voigt profile algorithms. The transfer equation is integrated with DELO-Bezier formal solvers in both scalar and Stokes-vector form. Speed is achieved through aggressive OpenMP parallelisation, adaptive per-line wavelength windowing, and a memory-capped block-processing scheme that lets arbitrarily large line lists be handled within a user-defined RAM budget. The code synthesises spectra thousands of Å wide from line lists of $10^8$ molecular and atomic transitions in under a minute on a modern multi-core laptop while reproducing benchmark calculations from established codes. FastSpec combines the physical completeness of classical model atmosphere and spectrum synthesis codes with the speed required by large surveys and the polarised transfer needed for stellar magnetism studies into a single portable package.

cross.title: Accuracy of electric current inference assuming three-dimensional hydrostatic equilibrium
cross.summary: The chromospheric and coronal heating problem is among the major open questions in solar physics. Some of the possible mechanisms that can explain the rise in temperature that is needed to reproduce the observations require the estimation of electric currents. Since these depend on the spatial derivatives of the magnetic field components, it is necessary to obtain the full magnetic field vector from observational data in a 3D geometrical grid. We developed a new method to obtain the 3D geometrical configuration of the atmosphere using the approximation of hydrostatic equilibrium in three dimensions to determine the gas pressure and density as a function of optical depth, column mass, or geometrical distance. This development has been designed as an extension for any inversion code that outputs a stratification of temperature and gas pressure or density to enable the estimation of electric current densities from observations. We investigated our approach using a snapshot from a sunspot MHD simulation. The difference between the solver output and the simulation, taken as the ground truth, is mostly between 30 and 45 %, showing a similar pattern over a large optical depth range. Additional tests also showed that the solver provides a unique solution, has a scarce sensitivity to the boundary condition and is only marginally impacted by the viewing angle. We conclude that the electric currents can be inferred at a reasonable accuracy with this approach using the simulation parameters as input. We also tested set-ups that aim at mimicking more realistic cases, where the code performed equally well. The results in this work show promise with respect to future applications to spectropolarimetric data, however, some additional challenges will need to be adressed when moving from the controlled input of the simulation to observational data.

cross.title: Forward model of the Gaia DR3 selection function
cross.summary: The completeness of an astronomical catalogue depends on its selection function, which is a combination of the observing strategy, instrumental characteristics, and intrinsic properties of the sources being observed. This is particularly complex for Gaia, whose non-uniform scanning law and onboard prioritisation of bright sources in dense areas make its selection function vary strongly with celestial position and source brightness. We estimate the Gaia DR3 source catalogue selection function across the whole sky and over the full magnitude range, using only data from the Gaia catalogue and knowledge of the nominal scanning law as provided by the Gaia Observation Forecast Tool. We develop a hierarchical Bayesian model that estimates the number of times Gaia scanned each celestial position jointly with the source detection efficiency, and fit it via Markov chain Monte Carlo to the 1 806 196 447 sources in Gaia DR3 with reported celestial positions, G magnitudes, and astrometric matched transit counts. Gaia DR3 is essentially complete for G in (5, 19.5) in the on-sky median. After that, the completeness decreases with magnitude according to the scanning law pattern combined with the imprint of crowded regions. The completeness is also lower at the very bright end of the survey, consistent with the known limitations on Gaia observations of bright stars. We find an unexpected completeness increase beyond G ~ 21, which we conclude is an artefact caused by extended sources, as confirmed by cross-matching against Euclid's Q1 catalogue. Treating the scanning law as part of the inference process, and anchoring it to all Gaia DR3 sources of all magnitudes on a fine-grained grid on the sky, removes the need for an explicit crowding correction. The resulting selection function, valid everywhere where Gaia data are available, is released as part of the GaiaUnlimited Python package. [abridged]

cross.title: ARENA: Active Region attENtion Aggregation for interpretable solar flare prediction
cross.summary: Predicting solar flares is a challenging space-weather forecasting problem with potentially significant impacts on Earth's upper atmosphere, including disruptions to radio communications. We propose Active Region attENtion Aggregation (ARENA), a neural network architecture that predicts solar flares from a variable number of active-region cutouts while learning to identify the region most relevant to the prediction. ARENA is trained using multiple-instance learning under weak supervision, requiring only a flare/no-flare label for the observation and no labels specifying the flare origin. The learned attention mechanism therefore provides a means of localizing the active region driving the prediction without explicit origin annotations. ARENA achieves a heidke skill score of 0.45 which is comparable to other flare prediction approaches. These results demonstrate that active-region-based aggregation can provide an efficient and interpretable approach to solar flare prediction. The code is available at this https URL .

cross.title: Physics Informed Neural Network for Multi-dimensional Turbulent Self-gravitating Flows
cross.summary: Molecular clouds exhibit complex, multi-scale dynamics driven by the interplay of turbulence, self-gravity, and gas pressure. Modelling these systems with conventional grid-based methods becomes increasingly expensive as spatial resolution and dimensionality increase. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative by incorporating the governing equations directly into the training objective, but their ability to model realistic turbulent self-gravitating flows remains largely unexplored. We apply PINNs to isothermal molecular clouds initialized with astrophysically motivated turbulent velocity fields, considering subsonic and supersonic evolution in two and three dimensions. We benchmark the predicted density and velocity fields against the finite-volume code Athena++. PINNs accurately recover the global evolution of the flow over multiple free-fall times across turbulent realizations, Mach numbers, and dimensionalities. Their training cost also exhibits weak dependence on spatial resolution, increasing by less than 25% from 128^3 to 1024^3 in our experiments. These results demonstrate that PINNs can model substantially more realistic self-gravitating turbulent flows than previously explored and provide a promising complementary framework for studying these systems.

cross.summary: We introduce a Python package called exoVetter that produces vetting metrics and visualizations to evaluate transiting exoplanet signals found in high-cadence time-series photometry. exoVetter is open source, modular, and independent of the mission data so that it can be easily expanded and used as part of different transit search pipelines tuned to different science cases and missions. We demonstrate its use in a pipeline as a way to distinguish real events found in a box-least squares exoplanet transit search of 324,530 light curves from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite mission; we limit our demonstration to stars also observed by the more sensitive Kepler telescope as a way to establish ground truth for the events found in the light curves. Using this ground truth, we provide baseline thresholds for several flux-level vetters and one centroid-offset vetter when using exoVetter metrics on TESS data. Our demonstration also indicates that it is possible to create a planet catalog from the light curves of dim targets (>13.5Tmag) that has a similar fraction of real events to that of the bright targets (<13.5Tmag) for short period events identified in the TESS-Gaia light curves.

repl.title: OmniSpectra: A Unified Foundation Model for Universal Spectra Representation Learning
repl.summary: Standard sequence models encode position by token rank rather than physical coordinate, typically forcing practitioners to destructively resample continuous physical signals such as spectra observed across heterogeneous instruments. We identify this coordinate mismatch as a structural limitation in cross-instrument representation learning, and propose OmniSpectra, a wavelength-native foundation model for spectral representation learning: a continuous-coordinate masked autoencoder that discards the integer pixel indexing of sequence modeling. Mapping physical coordinates to a logarithmic basis turns the multiplicative scaling induced by cosmological redshift into a uniform additive shift. In continuous rotary position embeddings, this shared shift cancels from relative token distances rather than producing grid-dependent positional distortion. We further counter the spectral bias inherent to implicit neural decoders with a physics-grounded, resolution-gated Fourier decoder that provides anti-aliasing. Pretrained on eight surveys and benchmarked against seven baselines, our model reaches state-of-the-art performance with only 12.2M parameters while outperforming substantially larger models, indicating that encoding physical structure can substitute for parameter scale.

repl.title: What visibility-graph curvature measures in Forbush decreases: a calibration on the two largest events of solar cycle 25
repl.summary: Discrete curvatures of visibility graphs are increasingly used as descriptors of geophysical time series, but their response to a transient has rarely been calibrated against the simplest properties of that transient. We carry out this calibration for the nodal Forman--Ricci curvature $\mathcal{F}$ of natural visibility graphs applied to neutron-monitor records of the Gannon storm (2024 May 10--11) and the 2025 June 1 Forbush decrease (FD), the two largest FDs of solar cycle 25, using 30-min NMDB data from six NM64 stations ($R_c \simeq 0$--$7$~GV), i.e.\ twelve station--event series. Curvature collapses at FD onset in every series (Cliff's $\delta = 0.63$--$1.0$), but a 6-h running standard deviation separates onset from quiet time more strongly (mean $\delta = 0.96$ vs $0.89$; mean block-permutation displacement $z = -27$ vs $-14$). Injecting synthetic decreases into the real pre-event records of each station shows that the curvature extreme follows $|\mathcal{F}_{\min}| \propto (A/\sigma)^{0.50}$ ($R^2 = 0.88$), where $A$ is the FD amplitude and $\sigma$ the station's quiet-time noise, and is independent of the duration of the main phase (exponent $0.006$ over 3--36~h). With $A$, $\sigma$ and the main-phase duration of each series as the only inputs, the calibration predicts the twelve observed extremes with standardized residuals of mean $-0.26$ and standard deviation $0.94$, and the observed extremes correlate with $A/\sigma$ at Spearman $\rho = 0.95$. Within the precision allowed by these data, nodal Forman--Ricci curvature of the whole-series visibility graph carries no information about these FDs beyond their amplitude relative to station noise; in particular, it does not distinguish the single-step Gannon decrease from the two-step June 2025 decrease.

repl.title: Euclid: Quick Data Release (Q1) -- Ultracool dwarfs in the Euclid Deep Fields
repl.summary: Ultracool dwarfs (UCDs) encompass the lowest-mass stars and brown dwarfs at the substellar boundary. These intrinsically faint objects are challenging to detect, but the wide coverage and deep sensitivity of the Euclid survey increase confirmed UCD counts by orders of magnitude. We carried out a systematic study using Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1) low-resolution near-infrared spectra to identify and characterise UCDs. A sample of previously known UCDs in Q1 validated the analysis, which was then applied to newly identified UCD candidates in Euclid Deep Field North (EDF-N; 22.9 deg^2, down to J_E ~ 24.5 mag). We confirm 33 new UCDs in EDF-N, spanning spectral types M7-T1 (J_E = 17-21 mag) and distances of 50-600 pc. Two objects were followed up with optical and NIR observations using the Gran Telescopio Canarias, providing independent validation of Euclid classifications. We determined spectral types for 33 new UCDs and 167 previously known UCDs by fitting SpeX Prism Library Analysis Toolkit standards. The known sample includes 103 Dark Energy Survey objects (M7-T0, J_E = 17-22 mag), 6 literature sources (M8-T7, J_E = 18-20 mag), and 58 Gaia sources (M7-L1, J_E = 17-24 mag). Independent stellar parameters from atmospheric model fitting agree well with Euclid spectral types. We also investigated Gaia UCDs in Q1 by combining mean XP spectra with Euclid NIR spectra to determine radii. We present a publicly available catalogue including observations, classifications, and stellar parameters. This work demonstrates Euclid's capability to characterise faint stellar populations, establishing a foundation for large-scale UCD studies.

repl.title: Quantitative modelling of type Ia supernovae spectral time series II: Exploring the diversity of thermonuclear explosion scenarios
repl.summary: Observations of type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) have led to suggestions of multiple progenitor and explosion scenarios. Distinguishing between scenarios and tying specific SNe Ia to individual scenarios however has so far been challenging. Constraints on the explosion physics are often achieved through empirical modelling of SNe Ia spectra and qualitative assessments of the level of agreement. While this approach has provided useful insights, it cannot be scaled up to large numbers of SNe Ia in a robust and systematic way. As a machine learning based framework for automated and quantitative fitting of SNe Ia, riddler is designed to overcome these limitations. Neural networks are used as radiative transfer emulators and, in conjunction with nested sampling, emulated spectra are fit to observations of SNe Ia to determine the best-fitting input parameters and explosion scenario. In this work, we present recent improvements to riddler, including a significantly expanded training dataset covering pure deflagrations, delayed detonations, double detonations, gravitationally confined detonations, and violent mergers. We show that despite the increased complexity and variety of our training data, riddler is able to accurately recover the input parameters and explosion scenario of spectra unseen during training. Using riddler, we fit observations of three SNe Ia covering different sub-classes: SN 2011fe, SN 2005hk, and SN 2018byg. We detail a number of limitations and assumptions that should be considered when applying similar approaches. Nevertheless, the benefits of this approach and riddler will result in automated fitting playing an increasingly important role in the coming years.

repl.title: UCLCHEM 4.0: An open source gas-grain astrochemistry simulation framework
repl.summary: Astrochemical modelling is a key tool for interpreting the formation and destruction of molecules in the interstellar medium, complementing the increasingly detailed observations enabled by modern day observational facilities. UCLCHEM is a comprehensive gas-grain astrochemical modelling framework that can compute the chemical evolution inside a parcel of gas and dust under a specified, time-dependent physical description. This allows both the post-processing of hydrodynamical simulations and the usage of physical parametrizations, ranging in context from extra-galactic to protoplanetary disk scales. The framework consists of a core routine that solves gas-grain chemical reaction networks as a function of time, self-consistently coupled to either a user-defined or parametrized physical evolution of density, temperature and other physical input parameters. The chemistry is solved with a rate-equation formalism, and includes a three phase description, namely gas phase, ice surface and bulk ice. This includes transport between the gas and ice phases via freeze-out, thermal and non-thermal desorption mechanisms, as well as a geometrical treatment of the growth and shrinkage of the surface and bulk chemistry. The framework includes parametrizations for astrochemical modelling of cloud collapses, protostellar cores and shocks as well as the ability to provide user-defined inputs. This release of the framework focuses on many quality-of-life-improvements, including an object-oriented Python interface, an upgrade from two phase to three phases and expanded support for post-processing of hydrodynamical simulations and user-defined parametrizations. This manuscript provides an overview of the physics and chemistry included in UCLCHEM, as well as the inner workings of the solver routine and the programming interface.

repl.summary: The in-Situ Thunderstorm Observer for Radiation Mechanisms (iSTORM) is a gamma-ray spectrometer to study gamma-ray transients originating from thunderstorms, such as glows and terrestrial gamma-ray flashes (TGFs). It is designed and built by the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory for deployment aboard a NASA ER-2 aircraft. Using an array of 32 one-inch-diameter $\mathrm{CeBr}_3$ scintillators read out with silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), the instrument achieves an energy range of $\sim 250 \ \mathrm{keV}$ to $5 \ \mathrm{MeV}$ under flight conditions, with a total geometrical area of $157 \ \mathrm{cm^2}$. One of two gamma-ray instruments in the ALOFT campaign, iSTORM recorded glows, terrestrial gamma-ray flashes (TGFs), and the newly discovered flickering gamma-ray flashes (FGFs).

repl.title: Tracing the Cosmic Origins: Machine Learning Reconstruction of the Primordial Density Field from EoR Observations
repl.summary: Reconstructing the initial conditions of the Universe from late-time tracers would unlock cosmological information buried by non-linear structure formation and astrophysics. We reconstruct the initial density field corresponding to $z=300$, with its linear amplitude extrapolated to $z=0$, from simulated 21-cm and CO(1-0) line-intensity maps at $z=8$ generated with LIMFAST. Using a three-dimensional U-Net, we reconstruct the initial conditions and evaluate their impact on cosmological parameter constraints. The two tracers probe complementary environments: 21-cm emission traces neutral, low-density regions of the IGM, while CO traces overdense, star-forming regions. We also train and evaluate the reconstruction on maps incorporating SKA1-Low- and COMAP-ERA-like instrumental response and thermal noise. In the noiseless case, combining both tracers delivers the most accurate reconstruction across ionisation states, with the cross-correlation coefficient between the reconstructed and true initial density fields, $|C(k)| \gtrsim 0.90$ for $k \lesssim 0.75\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$. With observational effects, small-scale information is degraded, but the joint reconstruction retains substantial large-scale coherence, with $|C(k)| \gtrsim 0.70$ for $k \lesssim 0.3\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$. We quantify cosmological information gains through simulation-based inference using power-spectrum summaries pre- and post-reconstruction. The largest improvements occur for $\sigma_8$ and $n_{\rm s}$, with a median aggregate marginal compression of $1.17$ bits in the noiseless case, corresponding to a $56\%$ reduction in the factorised product of prior-normalised $68\%$ marginal widths. With observational effects, the corresponding median compression is $1.29$ bits. These results demonstrate that joint 21-cm-CO reconstruction recovers cosmological information beyond pre-reconstruction summaries.

repl.title: Adding slow magnetoacoustic mode to the HLL-type multi-state approximate Riemann solution
repl.summary: Multi-state HLL-type approximate Riemann solutions of ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) typically assume that the medium within the Riemann fan is incompressible, and thus the slow magnetoacoustic mode cannot be included in their space-time wave configurations for the intermediate states. We propose a new strategy to design multi-state HLL-type solutions, allowing for the medium within the Riemann fan to be compressible. In particular, for the complete seven-wave configuration of the MHD Riemann problem, we estimate the slow magnetoacoustic speeds and a longitudinal flow speed between the slow modes, whose compressibility is estimated based on the relations between fast, Alfvén, and slow speeds. Then, following the conservation laws and Rankine-Hugoniot jump relations across the fast, Alfvén, and slow waves, we calculate all the intermediate states within the Riemann fan. Moreover, we discuss the solutions when certain wave modes degenerate, ensuring well-posedness and smooth transitions between complete and degenerate wave configurations. Numerical simulations using a Finite Volume solver show that the proposed approximate Riemann solution is less diffusive than the classic HLLD scheme, particularly for slow mode waves. For example, in a 1D test case with a strong longitudinal magnetic field, the new scheme needs one order of magnitude fewer grid cells compared to the classic HLLD scheme to resolve all wave modes.
